title: The Sons of Vinatā
body:
Thai Amāvāsyai is observed in the Tamizh calendar as Garuḍa Jayanti, the day of the appearance of Garuḍa, the divine vehicle of Sriman Nārāyaṇa.

The story of Garuḍa, told in the Ādi Parva of the Mahābhārata, is not merely the tale of a celestial eagle's immense power. It is a saga of bondage and liberation, rivalry and redemption, duty and devotion. In a way it foreshadows the great war of Kurukshetra, where the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, though of one family, fight a battle that shapes the course of the world. Just as the Mahābhārata unfolds as a war within a family, Garuḍa's story too turns on conflict born of kinship, deception, and an unrelenting pursuit of dharma.

It begins with the great rishi Kashyapa, whose penance and wisdom gave rise to many races of beings. Among his wives, two stood out: Kadrū and Vinatā. Kadrū, ambitious and calculating, wished for a thousand children. Vinatā, confident in her destiny, asked for only two, but wished that they would surpass all of Kadru's offspring. Kashyapa granted both their wishes. In due time Kadru's eggs hatched into a thousand Nāgas, while Vinatā's remained unhatched for a long time.

Impatience took root in Vinatā's heart. Unable to wait any longer, she broke open one of the eggs before its time. From it emerged Aruṇa, his upper body radiant like the sun, his lower body unformed. Though filled with divine brilliance, he was angered by his premature birth. He rebuked his mother for her haste and declared that, because of her impatience, she would become a servant; but he assured her that her second son, when he was born, would be her deliverer. With those words Aruṇa departed, and in time he became the eternal charioteer of Sūrya Deva, guiding his blazing chariot across the heavens.

Humbled by her mistake, Vinatā waited patiently for the second egg to hatch in its own time. When at last it did, the world beheld a being unlike any other. His wings stretched as vast as the sky, his feathers gleamed like molten gold, and his eyes burned with divine brilliance. This was Garuḍa, king of the birds, destined to challenge the might of the Devas and to soar beyond the reach of Indra himself.
